text: What does the acronym CIA stand for in information security?
options: Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability
Control, Inspection and Audit
Encryption, Identity and Authentication
Trust, Integrity and Anonymity

text: What is the main difference between a vulnerability and a threat?
options: A vulnerability is an exploitable weakness; a threat is what could exploit it
They are synonyms and are used interchangeably
A threat is a type of malware; a vulnerability is a misconfigured firewall
A vulnerability only exists in software; a threat only exists in hardware

text: Which security principle states that a user or process should have only the minimum permissions needed to do its task?
options: Defense in depth
Principle of least privilege
Separation of duties
Non-repudiation

text: What is a zero-day vulnerability?
options: A security flaw that has been publicly known for more than a year
A vulnerability that already has an official patch available
A flaw unknown to the vendor, with no patch available when it is exploited
A configuration error detected by an antivirus

text: What is 'defense in depth'?
options: Using a single, very robust security tool
Applying multiple layers of independent security controls
Encrypting only the network layer
Relying only on the firewall's perimeter security

text: Why is a long passphrase usually more secure than a short password with symbols?
options: Because it has more entropy by being longer, even if it uses simple words
Because passphrases can never be guessed by brute force
Because special symbols weaken security
Because systems don't allow short passwords

text: What is 'credential stuffing'?
options: An attack that tries username/password combinations leaked from other sites to access an account
A method for generating secure random passwords
A technique for encrypting passwords in the database
A type of firewall that blocks suspicious logins

text: In multi-factor authentication (MFA), what do 'something you know, something you have and something you are' represent?
options: The three types of firewall
The three layers of the OSI model related to login
The three classic categories of authentication factors
The three steps of a phishing attack

text: What is the purpose of adding a 'salt' when hashing passwords before storing them?
options: To speed up the login verification process
To prevent identical passwords from producing the same hash and to defeat attacks with precomputed tables (rainbow tables)
To compress the size of the stored hash
To make it easy to recover the original password

text: What is the main risk of reusing the same password on several sites?
options: None, as long as the password is long enough
If one site suffers a breach, an attacker can try that same password on your other accounts
Browsers automatically block reuse
It only affects the website's performance

text: What sets 'spear phishing' apart from generic phishing?
options: Spear phishing is targeted and personalized for a specific person or organization
Spear phishing only happens by phone
Generic phishing always includes attached malware
There is no real difference

text: What is 'pretexting' in social engineering?
options: Sending mass emails without personalizing them
Creating a false story or identity to gain the victim's trust and obtain information
A type of encryption used by attackers
Scanning a network's ports before an attack

text: What is the social engineering attack carried out by phone or voice messages called?
options: Smishing
Vishing
Whaling
Tailgating

text: Which of the following is NOT a typical sign of a phishing email?
options: Extreme urgency to act immediately
Sender domain slightly different from the official one
The email was verifiably digitally signed by the company
Links that don't match the expected domain when you hover over them

text: What is 'baiting' in social engineering?
options: Offering something attractive (like a USB drive or a free download) to induce the victim to compromise their security
Spying on conversations on social media
Sending advertising spam without malicious intent
Blocking access to a system until a ransom is paid

text: What is the main difference between a virus and a worm?
options: The worm spreads automatically across the network without needing a host file; the virus does need one
They are exactly the same
The virus only affects servers, the worm only affects personal computers
The worm cannot damage files

text: At a basic level, what does a firewall do?
options: Removes viruses already installed on the system
Filters and controls allowed network traffic according to defined rules
Encrypts all files on the hard drive
Automatically generates secure passwords

text: What characterizes a ransomware attack?
options: It encrypts the victim's files and demands a payment to restore them
It only steals passwords saved in the browser
It is a misconfigured type of firewall
It only affects email servers

text: What is a man-in-the-middle attack?
options: An attacker intercepts and potentially alters the communication between two parties without them noticing
An attacker floods a server with traffic until it goes down
An attacker installs a physical keylogger
An attacker guesses passwords by brute force

text: What does the use of HTTPS/TLS mainly protect in web communication?
options: The server's availability during outages
The confidentiality and integrity of data in transit, through encryption
The page's loading speed
The creation of automatic backups
